memory_boundary: All retained statements are model-memory research leads for source discovery only. No external search, repository Evidence search, current-provider lookup, standard verification or historical truth promotion was performed.

leads.memory: Hydrographic survey, sounding/bathymetry, shoreline and aids-to-navigation information pass through an official publication chain before reaching ships; the institutional chain matters because seabed or channel change is operationally useful only after authoritative processing and distribution.

Paper charts, sailing directions, light/list-type publications and electronic navigational products form a versioned information ecosystem rather than a one-time reference; vessel safety depends on having the applicable edition plus subsequent corrections.

Notices to Mariners, temporary/preliminary corrections and local or coastal navigational warnings are a recurring bridge between newly observed hazards or changes and the shipboard navigation picture; update latency itself is a researchable failure mode.

Electronic charting shifts correction work from manual chart marking toward licensed data, update packages, onboard ECDIS ingestion and configuration; digital distribution reduces some friction but introduces entitlement, version, integration and cyber/communications dependencies.

Chart datum, geodetic reference, tide/water-level reference and positioning-system assumptions can become dangerous when mismatched or misunderstood; a numerically precise position is not sufficient if the underlying reference frames differ.

Draft, tide, squat, channel depth, dredging status and survey recency combine into under-keel-clearance decisions; port access can therefore depend on information freshness as much as nominal berth or channel dimensions.

Weather routeing links meteorological and ocean forecasts with vessel characteristics, schedule, fuel use and safety limits; the operational output is a route/speed recommendation whose value depends on forecast quality, update cadence and master/operator decision rights.

Wind, waves and currents change speed-through-water, fuel burn and voyage time; route optimization can trade a longer geographic route for lower resistance, lower damage risk or a more reliable arrival time.

Ice charts, ice forecasts, route recommendations and local restrictions form a specialized navigation-information layer in seasonal waters; uncertainty can alter route choice, escort needs, waiting time and effective trading range.

Tropical-cyclone and severe-weather advisories drive avoidance, speed reduction, port departure/arrival timing and shelter decisions; the research value lies in decision timing and information vintage rather than cataloguing named storms.

Navigation information is only actionable if it reaches the vessel: satellite, radio, shore-system or onboard-network outages can leave a bridge team with stale products even when a newer warning exists ashore.

The last mile is procedural: officers must receive, apply, verify and cross-check chart, warning, weather and voyage-plan updates. Human workload and handover quality can therefore mediate otherwise sound information infrastructure.

A useful research record should preserve product identity, edition/update number, issue time, receipt time and application time because a later-correct chart or forecast must not be retroactively treated as known on the earlier voyage.

The atlas concept of effective versus nominal capacity extends to information: a physically available vessel and open port can still lose trading capacity through weather deviation, draft restrictions or delayed navigational updates.
The atlas fuel/speed tradeoff is forecast-conditioned rather than static: weather and current information can change the fuel-optimal speed and route on the same nominal voyage.

Port bottlenecks include hydrographic and navigation-information states such as shoaling, dredging, temporary depth limits, buoy changes or local warnings, not only berth queues and crane productivity.

The atlas known-time principle is especially important for navigational information because survey/event time, publication time, transmission time, onboard receipt time and application time can all differ.
Weather or physical conditions at chokepoints can force delay or route changes; this is already represented by the atlas chokepoint and effective-capacity leads.
Route deviation can raise sailing distance and tonne-miles; this is already represented by the atlas tonne-mile mechanism and is not a separate category here.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Recall can name some famous national offices but a directory would be uneven and low-value without Evidence.
Exact standard numbers, carriage dates and edition transitions are precision-fragile and deferred to Evidence.
Current vendor capability and market share require fresh source-first research and are outside atlas_only recall.
Attributing a grounding or casualty to stale charts, warnings or forecast use requires incident-specific Evidence.

method_observation.observation: Blind recall remains high-yield when information is treated as a versioned operational chain from observation through publication, transmission, receipt and application. It degrades when probing turns into standards, vendor or national-office cataloguing.

deferred_precision: exact hydrographic-office responsibilities and national publication practices
exact chart/ECDIS standard versions and carriage dates
current navigation-software or weather-routeing vendor capability
